Precious Metals Quarterly 2012 Q2 

# Chapter 3 Platinum 

## Good performance comes at a high price 

As of the end of the third week of June, platinum was trading 4% higher than this year’s opening London fix of $1,406/oz, making this the best-performing precious metal during the first half of 2012.  In fact, platinum is the only precious metal to have demonstrated a positive price performance through the first six months of this year. 

At the end of 2011, platinum looked very week, but some concerns about electricity and primary mine supply from South Africa, where national electricity utility Eskom warned of possible power shortages and Impala Platinum’s Rustenburg operations were paralysed by an unofficial strike, lifted sentiment in January and pushed the platinum price to a year-to-date high of $1,729/oz on 23 February. 

In the turmoil that followed the Federal Reserve’s comments at the end of February suggesting that QE3 might not yet happen, all four major precious metals prices plunged.  But platinum’s price descended at a slower pace than that of gold thanks to some support from the re-emergence of resource nationalism issues in Zimbabwe.  Indeed, platinum briefly recaptured a price premium over gold around mid-March for the first time since September 2011. 

While platinum had been trading below gold, many investors followed a sell-gold-buyplatinum strategy betting on the re-establishment of platinum’s traditional price premium.  And this had provided a little stronger support for this precious metal.  However, as soon as the strategy had borne fruit, investor interest evaporated and platinum lost much of its momentum. As a result, in the second half of the month, platinum weakened to a greater extent than gold and moved back into a discount. 

Renewed fears about the EU economy in combination with negative news from the European automotive market and reports of a slowdown in the Chinese economy continued to drag the platinum price lower during April and May.  By the end of May, platinum had effectively erased all of its gains for the year as its price dropped close to $1,400/oz. 

In early June, some South African platinum miners decided to cut production in response to low metal prices.  Their action caused a rebound in the platinum price which climbed to $1,460/oz at the end of the third week of June. 

Investment flows in platinum ETFs were mixed in the first half of 2012 and largely

mimicked the platinum price movements.  After being positive for the first two months of the year they weakened as economic sentiment worsened.  Europe’s preference is for diesel vehicles that still primarily use platinum-based autocatalysts, and the performance of the European auto market has been negative so far this year with the outlook for car sales in the coming months remaining bleak.  In addition, even taking into account the lost production in So

uth Africa due to earlier strikes and production stoppages, platinum has been and is still expected to be in a supply-demand surplus this year.  Together, these factors have so far provided weak incentives for investment.  Therefore it is of little surprise that over the first half of 2012, net ETF demand amounted to only 1.2 tonnes of platinum.  This compares with ETF demand of 4.1 tonnes over the same period in 2011 and 11.4 tonnes a year earlier. 

### Net fabrication demand for platinum may drop before things start to improve 

Net global fabrication demand for platinum in 2011 stood at 5,590 koz, according to the latest data compiled by _Johnson Matthey_ in March _._ This is 115 koz or 2% lower than the company envisioned back in November.  Despite the downward revision, net platinum consumption by industrial consumers still posted a positive growth of 3.1% from 5.420 koz in 2010, continuing its recovery from 2009.  As _Johnson Matthey_ is our primary statistical source, our own (gross) consumption estimates incorporate similar changes. 

_Johnson Matthey’s_ downgrading has affected demand estimates for nearly all industrial applications with the steepest drops seen in the jewellery and automotive sectors.  As a result, net demand in these sectors is now estimated to have fallen by 105 koz and 100 koz respectively from 2010.  However, these drops were not caused by any weakening of underlying demand – at the gross level year-on-year growth was actually registered in every industrial sector – but was rather a result of a higher than expected pick-up in platinum scrap supplies, driven principally by higher returns of end-of-life vehicle catalysts and old platinum jewellery pieces. Specifically, recycling of autocatalysts grew by 13% to 1,225 koz, while jewellery recycling rose by 10% to 810 koz. 

If last year’s growth in platinum recovery from autocatalysts was of little surprise as it had already become a part of a long and well-established trend (many cars scrapped in 2011 were manufactured in early 2000s when diesel-powered vehicles were gaining popularity and when Euro 3 came into force requiring higher platinum loadings), then the change in _Johnson Matthey’s_ view on the recycling of platinum jewellery was something we found particularly interesting.  The fact is that in its November review, the company did not expect any increases in platinum jewellery recycling.  Quite the opposite, the level of recycling was projected to fall by 15% to 690 koz.  In our view, the reason for such a significant revision could be some overordering of platinum stock by retailers and wholesalers when the metal started trading at a discount to gold in the third quarter of last year.  The jewellery trade might then have tried to capitalise on what it expected soon to be a re-establishment of platinum’s price premium over gold.  When, after a few weeks, it had become clear that such strategy was not bearing fruit, some jewellers will have been forced to liqui

date excessive stock of platinum by selling it back into the market.  As a result, net demand from this source fell by 0.9% against its 2010 level.

Precious Metals Quarterly 2012 Q2   Platinum 

111 

At the gross level, demand for platinum from autocatalyst producers was again stronger in 2011 than it had been in 2010; they bought 3,105 koz of platinum against 3,075 koz one year earlier.  The pace of the annual growth, however, slowed significantly and totalled just 1% compared with 41% posted in 2010.  This is perhaps not surprising as in many regions demand for new vehicles, particularly in the light duty sector, was badly affected by growing concerns over the state of health of the global economy and shaky consumer sentiment.  In addition, purchasing of platinum by Japanese car manufacturers dropped as they lowered output in the wake of the natural disaster which hit the nation in March of last year.  On top of that, the trend to introduce more palladium into diesel catalysts remained intact; according to _Johnson Matthey_ , palladium now accounts for some 30% of PGM demand in this sector, with some 50:50 Pt:Pd catalysts already in use. 

The negative effects of these factors, however, were fully offset by the strong growth in the purchasing of platinum in the heavy duty diesel sector.  As fleet operators, primarily in North America, returned to the market following the recession, large truck manufacturers increased platinum purchases by 27% from 400 koz in 2010 to 515 koz last year. 

The outlook for platinum demand in the auto sector in 2012 is mixed as one might expect with downbeat Eurozone sentiment weighing on automotive demand.  Because of deepening recession in large parts of Europe, regional car sales in the first five months of this year were nearly 8% lower than in the same period of 2011.  The outlook for the European economy has continued to darken and we maintain our negative stance on demand for platinum from local vehicle producers which we expect to fall this year by approximately 7% to 1,360 koz. 

The outlook for diesel vehicle demand (and hence for platinum) in the markets outside Europe remains more positive.  So far this year, diesel car sales have been very strong not only in Japan, where the economy is recovering quickly from last year’s disaster, but also in India, where diesel cars now account for about 40% of total sales.  And yet, the real story is the US market where we might be seeing the start of a golden era for diesel-powered cars; clean diesel sales were up 35% in the first quarter of 2012 over 2011 Q1 on the back of rising demand for more fuel-efficient cars spurred by higher fuel prices.  That said, at around 3%, the market share of diesel engines in the USA is still way below that in Europe where diesel vehicles occupy 52% of the local car market.  However, according to the latest estimates by the Bosch Group, the country will see diesels grab 10% of the national

market by 2015, five years earlier than it had previously expected. 

Meanwhile, for the first time, diesel engines’ share of the passenger car market in the UK climbed from 49.4% in the first four months of 2011 to 50.8% in the first four months of 2012. The upcoming introduction of Euro 6 engine emission legislation, which begins to come into force in January 2013, will also prompt the use of more platinum to treat NOx emissions from both heavy and light duty vehicles throughout Europe.  Even there, the outlook for automotive sector demand for platinum is therefore healthier than might be thought by simply looking at depressing European car sales figures.  For this reason, our forecast for platinum demand from this sector has remained largely unchanged. 

Demand for platinum from the glass manufacturing sector was among the few industrial applications for which _Johnson Matthey_ has revised its 2011 estimates upwards.  Ongoing rapid 

CRU International Limited confidential 

112 

Precious Metals Quarterly 2012 Q2   Platinum 

growth in demand for electronic goods equipped with LCD screens resulted in the construction and launch of new production lines in China and South-East Asia which in turn led to record levels of platinum purchasing by the glass sector.  As such, net platinum consumption soared by 44% to 555 koz in 2011, up from the 13% growth envisioned in September.  Such anomalous growth was a result of a significant amount of pre-buying which took place last year in anticipation of future expansion, particularly in Asia.  However, the global glass industry now finds itself struggling with overcapacity in terms of LCD and also fibreglass production, and we think that it might take a year or two before demand reaches a level where this extra capacity can be fully utilised and the need for further expansion reappears.  This expansion phase is likely to take place in 2014 and may spark a new surge in gross demand for platinum from this application.  Until then, however, we expect net platinum consumption from the glass manufacturing sector to remain subdued. 

According to _Johnson Matthey_ , latest data for 2011 platinum demand in most other industrial applications are much closer to the figures we were using as a basis for our forecasting in December. 

Anticipated weakness in demand from the global glass industry together with constantly increasing volumes of scrap metal emanating from this and other industrial applications, may undercut total net fabrication demand this year.  As such, we see net consumption in all applications except jewellery falling by 3.9% year-on-year to a total of 3,768 koz.  Based on an improving economic outlook, we expect net fabrication demand for platinum to start rising again beyond 2012, underpinned by growth in emerging economies and tighter regulations outlined in Euro 6 scheduled for introduction in 2013.  As such, net fabrication demand is now forecast to reach 5.16 Moz by 2016, an increase of 32% from

2011. 

### Global platinum mine supply is under pressure as platinum miners are struggling to increase output 

Platinum mine output is likely to be lower this year than we anticipated in March largely because of the rising likelihood that supplies from South Africa will post another annual decline.  The industrial relations climate in that country remains more than challenging and has led to further mine supply disruptions. 

Since our latest publication in March, South Africa’s platinum mining industry has continued to suffer from strike action.  During the March-April period, a three week long strike was seen at Modikwa, a joint venture between ARM and Anglo American Platinum.  The strike continued until the 10th of April and resulted in a loss of approximately 20 koz of PGMs.  In mid-May, disruption was again seen at Impala Platinum’s troubled Rustenburg mine where supporters of the National Union of Mineworkers (NUM) and the Association of Mineworkers and Construction Union (AMCU) clashed over dominance.  As a result, some 6 koz of platinum were added to the production lost from the Impala industrial unrest earlier this year when a strike reportedly cost the company 146 koz of metal. 

We expect further losses of platinum production due to strike action this year particularly given that the NUM will hold its leadership elections in June.  Additionally, other factors such as frequent Section 54 closures and steadily escalating operational expenses incurred by local 

CRU International Limited confidential 

Precious Metals Quarterly 2012 Q2   Platinum 

113 

miners in the form of higher energy charges, rising equipment costs and worker compensation continue to affect production volumes and eat into profits which, along with softening metal prices, will likely threaten the closure of higher cost mine sections and the future of smaller, marginal suppliers.  As such, we expect platinum production from South Africa to fall this year by even more than we thought in March.  We have made further downgrades to our projections and now expect national mine production to drop by 5.6% from 2011 levels to a total of 4.4 Moz compared with our March forecast of a 1.5% decline. 

However, it has not been all doom and gloom for the local platinum mining industry.  Some good news came from the South African government which announced its intention to invest rand 3.4 billion in platinum production based around the current Platmin Pilanesberg operation, the Sedibelo and Magazynskraal properties on the western limb of the Bushveld geological formation, with a further three exploration projects to the east, namely Mphahlele, Grootboom and Loskop.  The Pilanesberg operation has a planned capacity of roughly 250 koz/y of PGMs but the new entity, which is currently operating under a temporary name NewCo, has apparently targeted production of 1.1 Moz/y of PGMs within five years.  The operations are all relatively shallow with some being open pit and development cou

ld be relatively rapid, although we think that to meet this timescale and size of output will be extremely challenging. 

One interesting issue with the project is that the new company plans to use a hydrometallurgical process – the Kell process – rather than smelting in treating the ore to produce metal.  If this is successful, this could remove some of the problems related to the treatment of UG2 ore with its high chrome content.  It could also reduce energy usage, something that would be very useful in South Africa which is currently facing electricity supply issues and will do so over the next few years.  We do not have enough information about the process to assess its technical suitability for processing the PGMs but would like to caution that hydrometallurgical treatment of nickel laterite ores so far has proved to be much more difficult than was first anticipated. 

As for other platinum producing regions, last year’s surge in North American output was anomalous because mines were ramping up from earlier shutdowns and therefore it will not be repeated this year as there is not much spare capacity left.  Likewise, with less expansion planned within Zimbabwe, supplies of platinum are likely to be flat or even slip back this year as a reflection of the increasingly unfriendly business environment.  One of the latest developments in this area was the order issued by Zimbabwe’s central bank which prohibits the country’s banks from processing mineral exports by Implats’ local unit, accusing Zimplats of failing to comply with an order to bank locally.  Furthermore, Robert Mugabe, the Zimbabwean president, said that no new mining licences will be issued to foreign companies. 

Based on all of the recent production changes reported by platinum miners, we now expect global primary platinum production to dip this year by 4.5%, from 6,397 koz in 2011 to 6,110 koz.  This is more than we thought in March when output was expected to drop by only 1.2% to 6,320 koz of platinum. 

Meanwhile, the platinum industry continues to look outside its traditional regions of production in an attempt to minimise its geographical risk.  Apart from Zimbabwe, where indigenisation discussions may slowly be approaching a conclusion, North America appears to be becoming a more attractive location for PGM exploration.  In April, Wallbridge Mining 

CRU International Limited confidential 

114 

Precious Metals Quarterly 2012 Q2   Platinum 

announced the establishment of a new joint venture with Lonmin over its North Range property in the Sudbury region of Ontario.  At almost the same time, Impala agreed to vest its 50% interest in Wallbridge’s nearby Parkin Offset property.  Since then, Northern Shield, another smaller company, has signed a joint venture agreement with Impala too, on its Idefix property in Quebec.  We do not know how likely these projects are to come to fruition, but they make clear the industry’s desire to diversify its production base in geographical ter

ms and its belief in a positive outlook for PGM demand. 

As for the current year, the majority of existing platinum mines continue to underperform as has been reflected in operational updates released by the miners for 2012 Q1: 



- In the first quarter, **Anglo American Platinum** posted a 24% decline in its refined platinum production to 403 koz, down from 533 koz in the same period of last year.  This was an even larger 43% fall from the 710 koz reported in September-December.  The dramatic drop in production was ascribed to the continued occurrence of safety-related work stoppages and to a period of planned maintenance at its smelter.  Production often suffers in the first quarter because of the effect of year-end holidays.  Management has stated, nevertheless, that its earlier projections for a total of 2.6 Moz of refined platinum in 2012 will be achieved.  Anglo produced a total of 2.53 Moz in its fiscal year ending December 2011.  The company is currently reviewing its business in order to increase profitability and may or may not sell or close some of the mines which are less profitable. 



- **Impala Platinum’s** platinum output fell 46% or 195 koz in the three months to the end of March compared with the same period of last year.  Production at the company’s strike-hit Rustenburg operations declined by 146 koz to 76 koz in the March quarter.  The loss of 120 koz of platinum due to a six-week strike in February-March was exacerbated by rampup losses of 21 koz and Section 54 stoppage losses of 5 koz.  The company expected to return to full production in June. 



- **Aquarius Platinum** has warned that its full-year production could fall short of expectations as a result of work stoppages.  The firm says that output of PGMs could be 40 koz down on its February projection of 440 koz.  In 2011 Q1, the company reported a 20% drop in PGM production compared with the same period last year.  Output was down to 97,802 oz from 122,213 oz previously.  The production figure was also 7% down on the quarter to the end of December 2011, when 105,629 oz were recorded.  Among the reasons the management gave for the drop in output were weaker metal prices, a drop in production on the back of poor ground conditions, continuing safety stoppages and worse than usual absenteeism after the Christmas holidays. 

- In early June, Aquarius and Anglo agreed to idle the No. 4 shaft at their jointly owned Marikana mine in South Africa after a decline in metal prices made these operations economically unviable.  In addition, Aquarius placed the Marikana concentrator on care and maintenance.  The No. 1 and No. 2 shafts at the mine are already closed. 

- In mid-June, Aquarius closed its second South African mine, Everest, in an effort to conserve cash.  The company blamed strikes and depressed platinum prices which had made this operation unprofitable. 



- **Xstrata** saw a 16% decrease in PGM production at its South African operations in the 

CRU International

Limited confidential 

Precious Metals Quarterly 2012 Q2   Platinum 

115 

quarter to March with an outturn of 31,447 oz PGMs versus 37,430 oz in the comparable 2011 period.  The decline was again ascribed to problems at its wholly owned Eland mine which included earlier difficulties gaining government approval to extend mining of the open pit operation.  Management had decided to phase out the open pit operation at Eland in the final quarter of last year and to concentrate development efforts on the underground operation.  The plan is for the sinking of two new decline shafts at Eland that could contribute upwards of 150 koz/y of platinum by the end of 2013, and reach targeted output of 300 koz/y of platinum by late 2015. 



- **Eastern Platinum** reported a 25% increase in production in the first three months of the year from the last quarter of 2011.  Output from its Crocodile River Mine was up from 19,854 oz to 24,474 oz PGM, although the figure was down on the same period of last year.  In addition to the larger Zandfontein mine at Crocodile River, the re-start of operations at the adjacent Crocette mine, which was put on hold in December 2011, has been scheduled for 2013.  At the end of May, the company announced it was suspending funding for the ongoing development of the Mareesburg open pit mine and construction of the Kennedy's Vale concentrator plant, citing continuing low PGM prices and changes in the global economic environment and the operating environment in South Africa. 



- **Atlatsa Resources** , formerly known as Anooraq Resources, produced 27,799 oz of PGMs at its Bokoni mine in the first quarter.  This was a 24% increase from 22,500 oz produced in the March 2011 quarter but a 5% decline from its December quarter’s output of 29,316 oz. According to the company, production was negatively impacted by a mine fatality, as well as a number of Section 54 safety stoppages, which resulted in six operating shifts being lost during the period. 



- **Sylvania Platinum’s** dump operations were adversely affected during the first quarter by a four-week strike at the host mines in the Bushveld complex, unusually severe weather conditions and safety related stoppages.  The reduction in processing days resulted in PGM production for the quarter ended 31 March 2012 totalling 7,506 oz, or over 30% below the corresponding period of last year. 



- **Royal Bafokeng Platinum’s** first-quarter production was 10% down on last year’s figures, with platinum output totalling 38,426 oz.  The company blamed the fall in output on an increase in Section 54 related stoppages and higher turnover of rock drill operators, as a result of industrial action at neighbouring mines. 



- **Platinum Australia** has announced that it will review the viability of its Smokey Hills mine in South Africa, citing technical difficulties and weak PGM prices as reasons for a possible cutback. 



- **Zimplats** , the Zimbabwean arm of Impala Platinum, saw a 2% drop in

production in the three months to the end of March.  Output slipped from 97,174 oz 4E PGM in the December quarter to 94,321 oz in the first three months of this year.  This was still 6% up on the first quarter of 2011, when metal in concentrate output stood at 89,260 oz. 



- South Africa’s Department of Mineral Resources has granted **Platinum Group Metals** a mining right for its WBJV Project 1 platinum mine.  The mine, located north of Rustenburg, is expected to produce 275 koz/y combined platinum, palladium, rhodium and gold.

Precious Metals Quarterly 2012 Q2   Platinum 

Commencement of the south box cut for underground access and the start of phase 2 construction are planned for the second quarter of 2012. 



- **Norilsk Nickel** has reported a fall in PGM production in the first quarter of the year.  The company produced 166 koz of platinum, which was down 2%, or 4 koz, from the first quarter of 2011.  Although output was down in its core Russian divisions, there was an uplift in platinum and palladium production at its African operations, albeit from a considerably lower base. 



- Platinum production at **Vale** fell 33% in the first quarter when compared to the same period last year as the company suspended operations at all five of its mines in Sudbury for one week during the period due to the death of a worker, the fourth fatality in seven months.  For the March period, Vale produced 38 koz of platinum against 57 koz in the March 2011 period and 41 koz in the December 2011 quarter. 



- Starting from March, **Quadra FNX Mining Ltd** has operated under the name KGHM International Ltd, a subsidiary of KGHM Polska Miedź S.A. 



- The Frischgewaagd-Ledig mine, owned by **Wesizwe Platinum** and the **Jinchuan Group** , has been renamed Bakubung.  Main shaft commissioning is planned for April 2018 with production build up shortly thereafter.  Full production is expected to be achieved in 2023. 

### The platinum market keeps tightening 

We have revised our March estimates for this year’s platinum mine supply and fabrication demand downwards in order to reflect the challenges that platinum market continues to face. Specifically, we have lowered our platinum production forecast for this year by 210 koz or approximately 2.8% to 6,110 koz and cut our forecast for net fabrication demand by 235 koz or approximately 4% to 5,573 koz.  Since the reduction in demand exceeds that in supply, the residual of 25 koz has been added to our estimate of 2012’s surplus boosting the total figure to 537 koz from the 512 koz we forecast in March.  Despite this small increase, the size of the surplus is still expected to be 30% lower than the 807 koz registered in 2011 (revised up from 692 koz in March), assuming of course that net fabrication demand does not also contract more than anticipated. 

While the Euro crisis persists, it is hard to imagine significantly stronger vehicle sales across Europe, and the

refore overall platinum demand is likely to remain lacklustre in the immediate term. So, we have lowered our platinum price forecast for calendar 2012 and now expect platinum to average $1,600/oz this year. However, if the platinum miners start cutting production more aggressively in the second half of this year in response to the present low price environment, our outlook for the year may become less bearish. In 2013, platinum mine production is expected to resume growth and reach 6.2 Moz based in part on expansion plans already in the pipeline. However, we believe that the ongoing operational issues in South Africa and lack of investment in production and capacity are unlikely to lead to significant production increases going forward, suggesting that the platinum market may slip back into deficit in 2015 as the global economy starts to stabilise through the coming years pushing net fabrication demand higher. As a result, in the final year of our outlook, the platinum market should find itself in a deficit of approximately 138 koz.
